   31 | """``statsutils`` provides tools aimed primarily at descriptive
   32 | statistics for data analysis, such as :func:`mean` (average),
   33 | :func:`median`, :func:`mode`, :func:`variance`, and many others,
   34 | 
   35 | The :class:`Stats` type provides all the main functionality of the
   36 | ``statsutils`` module. A :class:`Stats` object wraps a given dataset,
   37 | providing all statistical measures as property attributes. These
   38 | attributes cache their results, which allows efficient computation of
   39 | multiple measures, as many measures rely on other measures. For
   40 | example, relative standard deviation (:attr:`Stats.rel_std_dev`)
   41 | relies on both the mean and standard deviation. The Stats object
   42 | caches those results so no rework is done.
   43 | 
   44 | The :class:`Stats` type's attributes have module-level counterparts for
   45 | convenience when the computation reuse advantages do not apply.
   46 | 
   47 | >>> stats = Stats(range(42))
   48 | >>> stats.mean
   49 | 20.5
   50 | >>> mean(range(42))
   51 | 20.5
   52 | 
   53 | Statistics is a large field, and ``statsutils`` is focused on a few
   54 | basic techniques that are useful in software. The following is a brief
   55 | introduction to those techniques. For a more in-depth introduction,
   56 | `Statistics for Software
   57 | <https://www.paypal-engineering.com/2016/04/11/statistics-for-software/>`_,
   58 | an article I wrote on the topic. It introduces key terminology vital
   59 | to effective usage of statistics.
   60 | 
   61 | Statistical moments
   62 | -------------------
   63 | 
   64 | Python programmers are probably familiar with the concept of the
   65 | *mean* or *average*, which gives a rough quantitiative middle value by
   66 | which a sample can be can be generalized. However, the mean is just
   67 | the first of four `moment`_-based measures by which a sample or
   68 | distribution can be measured.
   69 | 
   70 | The four `Standardized moments`_ are:
   71 | 
   72 |   1. `Mean`_ - :func:`mean` - theoretical middle value
   73 |   2. `Variance`_ - :func:`variance` - width of value dispersion
   74 |   3. `Skewness`_ - :func:`skewness` - symmetry of distribution
   75 |   4. `Kurtosis`_ - :func:`kurtosis` - "peakiness" or "long-tailed"-ness
   76 | 
   77 | For more information check out `the Moment article on Wikipedia`_.
   78 | 
   79 | .. _moment: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moment_(mathematics)
   80 | .. _Standardized moments: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standardized_moment
   81 | .. _Mean: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mean
   82 | .. _Variance: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Variance
   83 | .. _Skewness: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skewness
   84 | .. _Kurtosis: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kurtosis
   85 | .. _the Moment article on Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moment_(mathematics)
   86 | 
   87 | Keep in mind that while these moments can give a bit more insight into
   88 | the shape and distribution of data, they do not guarantee a complete
   89 | picture. Wildly different datasets can have the same values for all
   90 | four moments, so generalize wisely.
   91 | 
   92 | Robust statistics
   93 | -----------------
   94 | 
   95 | Moment-based statistics are notorious for being easily skewed by
   96 | outliers. The whole field of robust statistics aims to mitigate this
   97 | dilemma. ``statsutils`` also includes several robust statistical methods:
   98 | 
   99 |   * `Median`_ - The middle value of a sorted dataset
  100 |   * `Trimean`_ - Another robust measure of the data's central tendency
  101 |   * `Median Absolute Deviation`_ (MAD) - A robust measure of
  102 |     variability, a natural counterpart to :func:`variance`.
  103 |   * `Trimming`_ - Reducing a dataset to only the middle majority of
  104 |     data is a simple way of making other estimators more robust.
  105 | 
  106 | .. _Median: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Median
  107 | .. _Trimean: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trimean
  108 | .. _Median Absolute Deviation: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Median_absolute_deviation
  109 | .. _Trimming: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trimmed_estimator
  110 | 
  111 | 
  112 | Online and Offline Statistics
  113 | -----------------------------
  114 | 
  115 | Unrelated to computer networking, `online`_ statistics involve
  116 | calculating statistics in a `streaming`_ fashion, without all the data
  117 | being available. The :class:`Stats` type is meant for the more
  118 | traditional offline statistics when all the data is available. For
  119 | pure-Python online statistics accumulators, look at the `Lithoxyl`_
  120 | system instrumentation package.
  121 | 
  122 | .. _Online: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Online_algorithm
  123 | .. _streaming: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Streaming_algorithm
  124 | .. _Lithoxyl: https://github.com/mahmoud/lithoxyl
  125 |

  158 |     statistical datapoints for calculations such as mean, median, and
  159 |     variance.

  165 |             statistical measure is not defined. 0.0 by default, but
  166 |             ``float('nan')`` is appropriate for stricter applications.
  167 |         use_copy (bool): By default Stats objects copy the initial
  168 |             data into a new list to avoid issues with
  169 |             modifications. Pass ``False`` to disable this behavior.
  170 |         is_sorted (bool): Presorted data can skip an extra sorting
  171 |             step for a little speed boost. Defaults to False.

  173 |     """

  176 |         self._is_sorted = is_sorted

  178 |             self.data = list(data)
  179 |         else:
  180 |             self.data = data

  182 |         self.default = default
  183 |         cls = self.__class__

  185 |                                  if isinstance(getattr(cls, a, None),
  186 |                                                _StatsProperty)]

  195 |     def _get_sorted_data(self):

  197 |         sorted, but we do it lazily using this method, in case no
  198 |         sorted measures are used. I.e., if median is never called,
  199 |         sorting would be a waste.
  200 | 
  201 |         When not using a copy, it's presumed that all optimizations
  202 |         are on the user.
  203 |         """
  204 |         if not self._use_copy:
  205 |             return sorted(self.data)
  206 |         elif not self._is_sorted:
  207 |             self.data.sort()

  210 |     def clear_cache(self):

  212 |         that can be reused. For instance, accessing the ``std_dev``
  213 |         attribute after the ``variance`` attribute will be
  214 |         significantly faster for medium-to-large datasets.
  215 | 
  216 |         If you modify the object by adding additional data points,
  217 |         call this function to have the cached statistics recomputed.
  218 | 
  219 |         """
  220 |         for attr_name in self._prop_attr_names:
  221 |             attr_name = getattr(self.__class__, attr_name).internal_name
  222 |             if not hasattr(self, attr_name):
  223 |                 continue
  224 |             delattr(self, attr_name)

  486 |     def _get_quantile(sorted_data, q):

  490 |         if idx_f == idx_c:
  491 |             return data[idx_f]
  492 |         return (data[idx_f] * (idx_c - idx)) + (data[idx_c] * (idx - idx_f))

  498 |         maximum. ``0.5`` represents the median:

  500 |         >>> Stats(range(100)).get_quantile(0.5)

  505 |             raise ValueError('expected q between 0.0 and 1.0, not %r' % q)

  563 |         len_data, min_data, max_data = len(data), min(data), max(data)
  564 | 
  565 |         if len_data < 4:

  567 |                 count = len_data
  568 |             dx = (max_data - min_data) / float(count)
  569 |             bins = [min_data + (dx * i) for i in range(count)]
  570 |         elif count is None:
  571 |             # freedman algorithm for fixed-width bin selection
  572 |             q25, q75 = self.get_quantile(0.25), self.get_quantile(0.75)
  573 |             dx = 2 * (q75 - q25) / (len_data ** (1 / 3.0))
  574 |             if dx == 0:
  575 |                 return [float(min_data), float(max_data)] if with_max else [float(min_data)]
  576 |             bin_count = max(1, int(ceil((max_data - min_data) / dx)))
  577 |             bins = [min_data + (dx * i) for i in range(bin_count + 1)]
  578 |             bins = [b for b in bins if b < max_data]
  579 |         else:

  581 |             bins = [min_data + (dx * i) for i in range(count)]

  588 |     def get_histogram_counts(self, bins=None, **kw):
  589 |         """Produces a list of ``(bin, count)`` pairs comprising a histogram of
  590 |         the Stats object's data, using fixed-width bins. See
  591 |         :meth:`Stats.format_histogram` for more details.
  592 | 
  593 |         Args:
  594 |             bins (int): maximum number of bins, or list of
  595 |                 floating-point bin boundaries. Defaults to the output of
  596 |                 Freedman's algorithm.
  597 |             bin_digits (int): Number of digits used to round down the
  598 |                 bin boundaries. Defaults to 1.
  599 | 
  600 |         The output of this method can be stored and/or modified, and
  601 |         then passed to :func:`statsutils.format_histogram_counts` to
  602 |         achieve the same text formatting as the
  603 |         :meth:`~Stats.format_histogram` method. This can be useful for
  604 |         snapshotting over time.
  605 |         """
  606 |         bin_digits = int(kw.pop('bin_digits', 1))
  607 |         if kw:
  608 |             raise TypeError('unexpected keyword arguments: %r' % kw.keys())
  609 | 
  610 |         if not bins:
  611 |             bins = self._get_bin_bounds()
  612 |         else:
  613 |             try:
  614 |                 bin_count = int(bins)
  615 |             except TypeError:
  616 |                 try:
  617 |                     bins = [float(x) for x in bins]
  618 |                 except Exception:
  619 |                     raise ValueError('bins expected integer bin count or list'
  620 |                                      ' of float bin boundaries, not %r' % bins)

  631 |         idxs = [bisect.bisect(bins, d) - 1 for d in self.data]
  632 |         count_map = Counter(idxs)

  638 |     def format_histogram(self, bins=None, **kw):
  639 |         """Produces a textual histogram of the data, using fixed-width bins,
  640 |         allowing for simple visualization, even in console environments.
  641 | 
  642 |         >>> data = list(range(20)) + list(range(5, 15)) + [10]
  643 |         >>> print(Stats(data).format_histogram(width=30))
  644 |          0.0:  5 #########
  645 |          4.4:  8 ###############
  646 |          8.9: 11 ####################
  647 |         13.3:  5 #########
  648 |         17.8:  2 ####
  649 | 
  650 |         In this histogram, five values are between 0.0 and 4.4, eight
  651 |         are between 4.4 and 8.9, and two values lie between 17.8 and
  652 |         the max.
  653 | 
  654 |         You can specify the number of bins, or provide a list of
  655 |         bin boundaries themselves. If no bins are provided, as in the
  656 |         example above, `Freedman's algorithm`_ for bin selection is
  657 |         used.
  658 | 
  659 |         Args:
  660 |             bins (int): Maximum number of bins for the
  661 |                 histogram. Also accepts a list of floating-point
  662 |                 bin boundaries. If the minimum boundary is still
  663 |                 greater than the minimum value in the data, that
  664 |                 boundary will be implicitly added. Defaults to the bin
  665 |                 boundaries returned by `Freedman's algorithm`_.
  666 |             bin_digits (int): Number of digits to round each bin
  667 |                 to. Note that bins are always rounded down to avoid
  668 |                 clipping any data. Defaults to 1.

  671 |                3.3+, or 80 if that is not available.

  678 |         is used by format_histogram. The :meth:`~Stats.describe`
  679 |         method is another useful summarization method, albeit less
  680 |         visual.

  682 |         .. _Freedman's algorithm: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedman%E2%80%93Diaconis_rule
  683 |         """
  684 |         width = kw.pop('width', None)
  685 |         format_bin = kw.pop('format_bin', None)

  688 |                                        width=width,
  689 |                                        format_bin=format_bin)

  691 |     def describe(self, quantiles=None, format=None):

  697 |                 quantiles in the resulting summary. All values must be

  699 |                 ``[0.25, 0.5, 0.75]``, representing the standard
  700 |                 quartiles.
  701 |             format (str): Controls the return type of the function,
  702 |                 with one of three valid values: ``"dict"`` gives back

  704 |                 values. ``"list"`` is a list of key-value pairs in an

  706 |                 table. ``"text"`` converts the values to text suitable
  707 |                 for printing, as seen below.
  708 | 
  709 |         Here is the information returned by a default ``describe``, as
  710 |         presented in the ``"text"`` format:
  711 | 
  712 |         >>> stats = Stats(range(1, 8))
  713 |         >>> print(stats.describe(format='text'))
  714 |         count:    7
  715 |         mean:     4.0
  716 |         std_dev:  2.0
  717 |         mad:      2.0
  718 |         min:      1
  719 |         0.25:     2.5
  720 |         0.5:      4
  721 |         0.75:     5.5
  722 |         max:      7
  723 | 
  724 |         For more advanced descriptive statistics, check out my blog
  725 |         post on the topic `Statistics for Software
  726 |         <https://www.paypal-engineering.com/2016/04/11/statistics-for-software/>`_.
  727 | 
  728 |         """
  729 |         if format is None:
  730 |             format = 'dict'

  732 |             raise ValueError('invalid format for describe,'
  733 |                              ' expected one of "dict"/"list"/"text", not %r'
  734 |                              % format)
  735 |         quantiles = quantiles or [0.25, 0.5, 0.75]
  736 |         q_items = []
  737 |         for q in quantiles:
  738 |             q_val = self.get_quantile(q)
  739 |             q_items.append((str(q), q_val))
  740 | 
  741 |         items = [('count', self.count),
  742 |                  ('mean', self.mean),
  743 |                  ('std_dev', self.std_dev),
  744 |                  ('mad', self.mad),
  745 |                  ('min', self.min)]

  751 |         elif format == 'list':

  753 |         elif format == 'text':

  759 | def describe(data, quantiles=None, format=None):

  761 |     for describing most data. See :meth:`Stats.describe` for more

  782 |     def stats_helper(data, default=0.0):

  785 |     return stats_helper

  792 |         if attr_name in ('mad',):  # convenience aliases
  793 |             continue
  794 |         func = _get_conv_func(attr_name)
  795 |         func.__doc__ = attr.func.__doc__
  796 |         globals()[attr_name] = func

  799 | del attr
  800 | del attr_name
  801 | del func

  807 |     them to this function.

  809 |     Args:

  811 |         width (int): Number of character columns in the text output,
  812 |             defaults to 80 or console width in Python 3.3+.
  813 |         format_bin (callable): Used to convert bin values into string
  814 |             labels.
  815 |     """
  816 |     lines = []
  817 |     if not format_bin:
  818 |         format_bin = lambda v: v
  819 |     if not width:
  820 |         try:
  821 |             import shutil  # python 3 convenience
  822 |             width = shutil.get_terminal_size()[0]
  823 |         except Exception:

  825 | 
  826 |     bins = [b for b, _ in bin_counts]
  827 |     count_max = max([count for _, count in bin_counts])
  828 |     count_cols = len(str(count_max))

  830 |     labels = ['%s' % format_bin(b) for b in bins]
  831 |     label_cols = max([len(l) for l in labels])
  832 |     tmp_line = '{}: {} #'.format('x' * label_cols, count_max)

  410 |         >>> round(left_skewed, 3), round(right_skewed, 3)

  425 |         distribution having a kurtosis of 3.

  427 |         http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kurtosis

  429 |         See the module docstring for more about statistical moments.
  430 | 
  431 |         >>> kurtosis(range(9))

  435 |         centrally distributed than the normal curve.
  436 |         """
  437 |         data, s_dev = self.data, self.std_dev
  438 |         if len(data) > 1 and s_dev > 0:
  439 |             return (sum(self._get_pow_diffs(4)) /
  440 |                     float((len(data) - 1) * (s_dev ** 4)))

  445 |     def _calc_pearson_type(self):
  446 |         precision = self._pearson_precision
  447 |         skewness = self.skewness
  448 |         kurtosis = self.kurtosis
  449 |         beta1 = skewness ** 2.0
  450 |         beta2 = kurtosis * 1.0
  451 | 
  452 |         # TODO: range checks?
  453 | 
  454 |         c0 = (4 * beta2) - (3 * beta1)
  455 |         c1 = skewness * (beta2 + 3)
  456 |         c2 = (2 * beta2) - (3 * beta1) - 6
  457 | 
  458 |         if round(c1, precision) == 0:
  459 |             if round(beta2, precision) == 3:
  460 |                 return 0  # Normal
  461 |             else:
  462 |                 if beta2 < 3:
  463 |                     return 2  # Symmetric Beta
  464 |                 elif beta2 > 3:
  465 |                     return 7
  466 |         elif round(c2, precision) == 0:
  467 |             return 3  # Gamma
  468 |         else:
  469 |             if c0 == 0:
  470 |                 # At exact zero, c2's sign selects the limiting Type I/VI.
  471 |                 return 1 if c2 < 0 else 6
  472 |             k = c1 ** 2 / (4 * c0 * c2)
  473 |             if k < 0:
  474 |                 return 1  # Beta
  475 |             # The existing precision also widens the Type V boundary.
  476 |             elif round(k, precision) == 1:
  477 |                 return 5  # Type V
  478 |             elif k < 1:
  479 |                 return 4  # Type IV
  480 |             else:
  481 |                 return 6  # Type VI
  482 |         raise RuntimeError('missed a spot')

  485 |     @staticmethod
  486 |     def _get_quantile(sorted_data, q):
  487 |         data, n = sorted_data, len(sorted_data)
  488 |         idx = q / 1.0 * (n - 1)
  489 |         idx_f, idx_c = int(floor(idx)), int(ceil(idx))
  490 |         if idx_f == idx_c:
  491 |             return data[idx_f]
  492 |         return (data[idx_f] * (idx_c - idx)) + (data[idx_c] * (idx - idx_f))
  493 | 
  494 |     def get_quantile(self, q):
  495 |         """Get a quantile from the dataset. Quantiles are floating point
  496 |         values between ``0.0`` and ``1.0``, with ``0.0`` representing
  497 |         the minimum value in the dataset and ``1.0`` representing the
  498 |         maximum. ``0.5`` represents the median:
  499 | 
  500 |         >>> Stats(range(100)).get_quantile(0.5)
  501 |         49.5
  502 |         """
  503 |         q = float(q)
  504 |         if not 0.0 <= q <= 1.0:
  505 |             raise ValueError('expected q between 0.0 and 1.0, not %r' % q)
  506 |         elif not self.data:
  507 |             return self.default
  508 |         return self._get_quantile(self._get_sorted_data(), q)
  509 | 
  510 |     def get_zscore(self, value):
  511 |         """Get the z-score for *value* in the group. If the standard deviation
  512 |         is 0, 0 inf or -inf will be returned to indicate whether the value is
  513 |         equal to, greater than or below the group's mean.
  514 |         """
  515 |         mean = self.mean
  516 |         if self.std_dev == 0:
  517 |             if value == mean:
  518 |                 return 0
  519 |             if value > mean:
  520 |                 return float('inf')
  521 |             if value < mean:
  522 |                 return float('-inf')
  523 |         return (float(value) - mean) / self.std_dev
  524 | 
  525 |     def trim_relative(self, amount=0.15):
  526 |         """A utility function used to cut a proportion of values off each end
  527 |         of a list of values. This has the effect of limiting the
  528 |         effect of outliers.
  529 | 
  530 |         Args:
  531 |             amount (float): A value between 0.0 and 0.5 to trim off of
  532 |                 each side of the data.
  533 | 
  534 |         .. note:
  535 | 
  536 |             This operation modifies the data in-place. It does not
  537 |             make or return a copy.
  538 | 
  539 |         """
  540 |         trim = float(amount)
  541 |         if not 0.0 <= trim < 0.5:
  542 |             raise ValueError('expected amount between 0.0 and 0.5, not %r'
  543 |                              % trim)
  544 |         size = len(self.data)
  545 |         size_diff = int(size * trim)
  546 |         if size_diff == 0.0:
  547 |             return
  548 |         self.data = self._get_sorted_data()[size_diff:-size_diff]
  549 |         self.clear_cache()

  551 |     def _get_pow_diffs(self, power):
  552 |         """
  553 |         A utility function used for calculating statistical moments.
  554 |         """
  555 |         m = self.mean
  556 |         return [(v - m) ** power for v in self.data]

  558 |     def _get_bin_bounds(self, count=None, with_max=False):
  559 |         if not self.data:
  560 |             return [0.0]  # TODO: raise?
  561 | 
  562 |         data = self.data
  563 |         len_data, min_data, max_data = len(data), min(data), max(data)
  564 | 
  565 |         if len_data < 4:
  566 |             if not count:
  567 |                 count = len_data
  568 |             dx = (max_data - min_data) / float(count)
  569 |             bins = [min_data + (dx * i) for i in range(count)]
  570 |         elif count is None:
  571 |             # freedman algorithm for fixed-width bin selection
  572 |             q25, q75 = self.get_quantile(0.25), self.get_quantile(0.75)
  573 |             dx = 2 * (q75 - q25) / (len_data ** (1 / 3.0))
  574 |             if dx == 0:
  575 |                 return [float(min_data), float(max_data)] if with_max else [float(min_data)]
  576 |             bin_count = max(1, int(ceil((max_data - min_data) / dx)))
  577 |             bins = [min_data + (dx * i) for i in range(bin_count + 1)]
  578 |             bins = [b for b in bins if b < max_data]
  579 |         else:
  580 |             dx = (max_data - min_data) / float(count)
  581 |             bins = [min_data + (dx * i) for i in range(count)]
  582 | 
  583 |         if with_max:
  584 |             bins.append(float(max_data))
  585 | 
  586 |         return bins
  587 | 
  588 |     def get_histogram_counts(self, bins=None, **kw):
  589 |         """Produces a list of ``(bin, count)`` pairs comprising a histogram of
  590 |         the Stats object's data, using fixed-width bins. See
  591 |         :meth:`Stats.format_histogram` for more details.
  592 | 
  593 |         Args:
  594 |             bins (int): maximum number of bins, or list of
  595 |                 floating-point bin boundaries. Defaults to the output of
  596 |                 Freedman's algorithm.
  597 |             bin_digits (int): Number of digits used to round down the
  598 |                 bin boundaries. Defaults to 1.
  599 | 
  600 |         The output of this method can be stored and/or modified, and
  601 |         then passed to :func:`statsutils.format_histogram_counts` to
  602 |         achieve the same text formatting as the
  603 |         :meth:`~Stats.format_histogram` method. This can be useful for
  604 |         snapshotting over time.
  605 |         """
  606 |         bin_digits = int(kw.pop('bin_digits', 1))
  607 |         if kw:
  608 |             raise TypeError('unexpected keyword arguments: %r' % kw.keys())
  609 | 
  610 |         if not bins:
  611 |             bins = self._get_bin_bounds()
  612 |         else:
  613 |             try:
  614 |                 bin_count = int(bins)
  615 |             except TypeError:
  616 |                 try:
  617 |                     bins = [float(x) for x in bins]
  618 |                 except Exception:
  619 |                     raise ValueError('bins expected integer bin count or list'
  620 |                                      ' of float bin boundaries, not %r' % bins)
  621 |                 if self.min < bins[0]:
  622 |                     bins = [self.min] + bins
  623 |             else:
  624 |                 bins = self._get_bin_bounds(bin_count)
  625 | 
  626 |         # floor and ceil really should have taken ndigits, like round()
  627 |         round_factor = 10.0 ** bin_digits
  628 |         bins = [floor(b * round_factor) / round_factor for b in bins]
  629 |         bins = sorted(set(bins))
  630 | 
  631 |         idxs = [bisect.bisect(bins, d) - 1 for d in self.data]
  632 |         count_map = Counter(idxs)
  633 | 
  634 |         bin_counts = [(b, count_map.get(i, 0)) for i, b in enumerate(bins)]
  635 | 
  636 |         return bin_counts
  637 | 
  638 |     def format_histogram(self, bins=None, **kw):
  639 |         """Produces a textual histogram of the data, using fixed-width bins,
  640 |         allowing for simple visualization, even in console environments.
  641 | 
  642 |         >>> data = list(range(20)) + list(range(5, 15)) + [10]
  643 |         >>> print(Stats(data).format_histogram(width=30))
  644 |          0.0:  5 #########
  645 |          4.4:  8 ###############
  646 |          8.9: 11 ####################
  647 |         13.3:  5 #########
  648 |         17.8:  2 ####
  649 | 
  650 |         In this histogram, five values are between 0.0 and 4.4, eight
  651 |         are between 4.4 and 8.9, and two values lie between 17.8 and
  652 |         the max.
  653 | 
  654 |         You can specify the number of bins, or provide a list of
  655 |         bin boundaries themselves. If no bins are provided, as in the
  656 |         example above, `Freedman's algorithm`_ for bin selection is
  657 |         used.
  658 | 
  659 |         Args:
  660 |             bins (int): Maximum number of bins for the
  661 |                 histogram. Also accepts a list of floating-point
  662 |                 bin boundaries. If the minimum boundary is still
  663 |                 greater than the minimum value in the data, that
  664 |                 boundary will be implicitly added. Defaults to the bin
  665 |                 boundaries returned by `Freedman's algorithm`_.
  666 |             bin_digits (int): Number of digits to round each bin
  667 |                 to. Note that bins are always rounded down to avoid
  668 |                 clipping any data. Defaults to 1.
  669 |             width (int): integer number of columns in the longest line
  670 |                in the histogram. Defaults to console width on Python
  671 |                3.3+, or 80 if that is not available.
  672 |             format_bin (callable): Called on each bin to create a
  673 |                label for the final output. Use this function to add
  674 |                units, such as "ms" for milliseconds.
  675 | 
  676 |         Should you want something more programmatically reusable, see
  677 |         the :meth:`~Stats.get_histogram_counts` method, the output of
  678 |         is used by format_histogram. The :meth:`~Stats.describe`
  679 |         method is another useful summarization method, albeit less
  680 |         visual.
  681 | 
  682 |         .. _Freedman's algorithm: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedman%E2%80%93Diaconis_rule
  683 |         """
  684 |         width = kw.pop('width', None)
  685 |         format_bin = kw.pop('format_bin', None)
  686 |         bin_counts = self.get_histogram_counts(bins=bins, **kw)
  687 |         return format_histogram_counts(bin_counts,
  688 |                                        width=width,
  689 |                                        format_bin=format_bin)
  690 | 
  691 |     def describe(self, quantiles=None, format=None):
  692 |         """Provides standard summary statistics for the data in the Stats
  693 |         object, in one of several convenient formats.
  694 | 
  695 |         Args:
  696 |             quantiles (list): A list of numeric values to use as
  697 |                 quantiles in the resulting summary. All values must be
  698 |                 0.0-1.0, with 0.5 representing the median. Defaults to
  699 |                 ``[0.25, 0.5, 0.75]``, representing the standard
  700 |                 quartiles.
  701 |             format (str): Controls the return type of the function,
  702 |                 with one of three valid values: ``"dict"`` gives back
  703 |                 a :class:`dict` with the appropriate keys and
  704 |                 values. ``"list"`` is a list of key-value pairs in an
  705 |                 order suitable to pass to an OrderedDict or HTML
  706 |                 table. ``"text"`` converts the values to text suitable
  707 |                 for printing, as seen below.
  708 | 
  709 |         Here is the information returned by a default ``describe``, as
  710 |         presented in the ``"text"`` format:
  711 | 
  712 |         >>> stats = Stats(range(1, 8))
  713 |         >>> print(stats.describe(format='text'))
  714 |         count:    7
  715 |         mean:     4.0
  716 |         std_dev:  2.0
  717 |         mad:      2.0
  718 |         min:      1
  719 |         0.25:     2.5
  720 |         0.5:      4
  721 |         0.75:     5.5
  722 |         max:      7
  723 | 
  724 |         For more advanced descriptive statistics, check out my blog
  725 |         post on the topic `Statistics for Software
  726 |         <https://www.paypal-engineering.com/2016/04/11/statistics-for-software/>`_.
  727 | 
  728 |         """
  729 |         if format is None:
  730 |             format = 'dict'
  731 |         elif format not in ('dict', 'list', 'text'):
  732 |             raise ValueError('invalid format for describe,'
  733 |                              ' expected one of "dict"/"list"/"text", not %r'
  734 |                              % format)
  735 |         quantiles = quantiles or [0.25, 0.5, 0.75]
  736 |         q_items = []
  737 |         for q in quantiles:
  738 |             q_val = self.get_quantile(q)
  739 |             q_items.append((str(q), q_val))
  740 | 
  741 |         items = [('count', self.count),
  742 |                  ('mean', self.mean),
  743 |                  ('std_dev', self.std_dev),
  744 |                  ('mad', self.mad),
  745 |                  ('min', self.min)]
  746 | 
  747 |         items.extend(q_items)
  748 |         items.append(('max', self.max))
  749 |         if format == 'dict':
  750 |             ret = dict(items)
  751 |         elif format == 'list':
  752 |             ret = items
  753 |         elif format == 'text':
  754 |             ret = '\n'.join(['{}{}'.format((label + ':').ljust(10), val)
  755 |                              for label, val in items])
  756 |         return ret
  757 |

  759 | def describe(data, quantiles=None, format=None):
  760 |     """A convenience function to get standard summary statistics useful
  761 |     for describing most data. See :meth:`Stats.describe` for more
  762 |     details.

  764 |     >>> print(describe(range(7), format='text'))

  776 |     summarization that uses textual visualization.

  123 | .. _streaming: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Streaming_algorithm
  124 | .. _Lithoxyl: https://github.com/mahmoud/lithoxyl

  134 | class _StatsProperty:
  135 |     def __init__(self, name, func):
  136 |         self.name = name
  137 |         self.func = func
  138 |         self.internal_name = '_' + name
  139 | 
  140 |         doc = func.__doc__ or ''
  141 |         pre_doctest_doc, _, _ = doc.partition('>>>')

  144 |     def __get__(self, obj, objtype=None):

  146 |             return self
  147 |         if not obj.data:
  148 |             return obj.default
  149 |         try:
  150 |             return getattr(obj, self.internal_name)
  151 |         except AttributeError:
  152 |             setattr(obj, self.internal_name, self.func(obj))
  153 |             return getattr(obj, self.internal_name)

  156 | class Stats:
  157 |     """The ``Stats`` type is used to represent a group of unordered
  158 |     statistical datapoints for calculations such as mean, median, and
  159 |     variance.
  160 | 
  161 |     Args:
  162 | 
  163 |         data (list): List or other iterable containing numeric values.
  164 |         default (float): A value to be returned when a given
  165 |             statistical measure is not defined. 0.0 by default, but
  166 |             ``float('nan')`` is appropriate for stricter applications.
  167 |         use_copy (bool): By default Stats objects copy the initial
  168 |             data into a new list to avoid issues with
  169 |             modifications. Pass ``False`` to disable this behavior.
  170 |         is_sorted (bool): Presorted data can skip an extra sorting
  171 |             step for a little speed boost. Defaults to False.
  172 | 
  173 |     """
  174 |     def __init__(self, data, default=0.0, use_copy=True, is_sorted=False):
  175 |         self._use_copy = use_copy
  176 |         self._is_sorted = is_sorted
  177 |         if use_copy:
  178 |             self.data = list(data)
  179 |         else:
  180 |             self.data = data
  181 | 
  182 |         self.default = default
  183 |         cls = self.__class__
  184 |         self._prop_attr_names = [a for a in dir(self)
  185 |                                  if isinstance(getattr(cls, a, None),
  186 |                                                _StatsProperty)]
  187 |         self._pearson_precision = 0
  188 | 
  189 |     def __len__(self):
  190 |         return len(self.data)
  191 | 
  192 |     def __iter__(self):
  193 |         return iter(self.data)
  194 | 
  195 |     def _get_sorted_data(self):
  196 |         """When using a copy of the data, it's better to have that copy be
  197 |         sorted, but we do it lazily using this method, in case no
  198 |         sorted measures are used. I.e., if median is never called,
  199 |         sorting would be a waste.
  200 | 
  201 |         When not using a copy, it's presumed that all optimizations
  202 |         are on the user.
  203 |         """
  204 |         if not self._use_copy:
  205 |             return sorted(self.data)
  206 |         elif not self._is_sorted:
  207 |             self.data.sort()
  208 |         return self.data
  209 | 
  210 |     def clear_cache(self):
  211 |         """``Stats`` objects automatically cache intermediary calculations
  212 |         that can be reused. For instance, accessing the ``std_dev``
  213 |         attribute after the ``variance`` attribute will be
  214 |         significantly faster for medium-to-large datasets.
  215 | 
  216 |         If you modify the object by adding additional data points,
  217 |         call this function to have the cached statistics recomputed.
  218 | 
  219 |         """
  220 |         for attr_name in self._prop_attr_names:
  221 |             attr_name = getattr(self.__class__, attr_name).internal_name
  222 |             if not hasattr(self, attr_name):
  223 |                 continue
  224 |             delattr(self, attr_name)
  225 |         return
  226 | 
  227 |     def _calc_count(self):

  229 |         :func:`len` on a Stats object, but provided for pandas terminology
  230 |         parallelism.
  231 | 
  232 |         >>> Stats(range(20)).count
  233 |         20
  234 |         """
  235 |         return len(self.data)
  236 |     count = _StatsProperty('count', _calc_count)

  238 |     def _calc_mean(self):
  239 |         """
  240 |         The arithmetic mean, or "average". Sum of the values divided by
  241 |         the number of values.
  242 | 
  243 |         >>> mean(range(20))
  244 |         9.5
  245 |         >>> mean(list(range(19)) + [949])  # 949 is an arbitrary outlier
  246 |         56.0
  247 |         """
  248 |         return sum(self.data, 0.0) / len(self.data)

  251 |     def _calc_max(self):
  252 |         """
  253 |         The maximum value present in the data.
  254 | 
  255 |         >>> Stats([2, 1, 3]).max
  256 |         3
  257 |         """
  258 |         if self._is_sorted:
  259 |             return self.data[-1]

  262 | 
  263 |     def _calc_min(self):

  265 |         The minimum value present in the data.
  266 | 
  267 |         >>> Stats([2, 1, 3]).min

  269 |         """
  270 |         if self._is_sorted:
  271 |             return self.data[0]

  275 |     def _calc_median(self):
  276 |         """
  277 |         The median is either the middle value or the average of the two
  278 |         middle values of a sample. Compared to the mean, it's generally
  279 |         more resilient to the presence of outliers in the sample.
  280 | 
  281 |         >>> median([2, 1, 3])
  282 |         2
  283 |         >>> median(range(97))
  284 |         48
  285 |         >>> median(list(range(96)) + [1066])  # 1066 is an arbitrary outlier
  286 |         48
  287 |         """
  288 |         return self._get_quantile(self._get_sorted_data(), 0.5)
  289 |     median = _StatsProperty('median', _calc_median)

  291 |     def _calc_mode(self):
  292 |         """
  293 |         The mode is the value that appears most frequently in the
  294 |         data. Unlike the mean and median, the mode is well-defined for
  295 |         non-numeric, categorical data, too.
  296 | 
  297 |         >>> mode([2, 1, 3, 1])
  298 |         1
  299 |         >>> mode(['a', 'b', 'b', 'c', 'c', 'c'])
  300 |         'c'

  302 |         When several values are equally common, the one appearing
  303 |         first in the data is returned, matching the standard library's
  304 |         :func:`statistics.mode`.
  305 | 
  306 |         >>> mode([1, 1, 2, 2, 3])
  307 |         1
  308 |         """
  309 |         return Counter(self.data).most_common(1)[0][0]

  312 |     def _calc_iqr(self):
  313 |         """Inter-quartile range (IQR) is the difference between the 75th
  314 |         percentile and 25th percentile. IQR is a robust measure of
  315 |         dispersion, like standard deviation, but safer to compare
  316 |         between datasets, as it is less influenced by outliers.
  317 | 
  318 |         >>> iqr([1, 2, 3, 4, 5])
  319 |         2
  320 |         >>> iqr(range(1001))
  321 |         500
  322 |         """
  323 |         return self.get_quantile(0.75) - self.get_quantile(0.25)
  324 |     iqr = _StatsProperty('iqr', _calc_iqr)

  326 |     def _calc_trimean(self):
  327 |         """The trimean is a robust measure of central tendency, like the
  328 |         median, that takes the weighted average of the median and the
  329 |         upper and lower quartiles.
  330 | 
  331 |         >>> trimean([2, 1, 3])
  332 |         2.0
  333 |         >>> trimean(range(97))
  334 |         48.0
  335 |         >>> trimean(list(range(96)) + [1066])  # 1066 is an arbitrary outlier
  336 |         48.0
  337 | 
  338 |         """
  339 |         sorted_data = self._get_sorted_data()
  340 |         gq = lambda q: self._get_quantile(sorted_data, q)
  341 |         return (gq(0.25) + (2 * gq(0.5)) + gq(0.75)) / 4.0
  342 |     trimean = _StatsProperty('trimean', _calc_trimean)

  344 |     def _calc_variance(self):
  345 |         """\
  346 |         Variance is the average of the squares of the difference between
  347 |         each value and the mean.
  348 | 
  349 |         >>> variance(range(97))
  350 |         784.0
  351 |         """

  353 |         return mean(self._get_pow_diffs(2))

  356 |     def _calc_std_dev(self):

  358 |         Standard deviation. Square root of the variance.
  359 | 
  360 |         >>> std_dev(range(97))

  362 |         """

  366 |     def _calc_median_abs_dev(self):

  368 |         Median Absolute Deviation is a robust measure of statistical

  370 | 
  371 |         >>> median_abs_dev(range(97))
  372 |         24.0
  373 |         """
  374 |         global median  # defined elsewhere in this file
  375 |         sorted_vals = sorted(self.data)
  376 |         x = float(median(sorted_vals))
  377 |         return median([abs(x - v) for v in sorted_vals])

  381 |     def _calc_rel_std_dev(self):
  382 |         """\
  383 |         Standard deviation divided by the absolute value of the average.
  384 | 
  385 |         http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Relative_standard_deviation
  386 | 
  387 |         >>> print('%1.3f' % rel_std_dev(range(97)))
  388 |         0.583
  389 |         """

  391 |         if abs_mean:
  392 |             return self.std_dev / abs_mean
  393 |         else:
  394 |             return self.default

  397 |     def _calc_skewness(self):

  399 |         Indicates the asymmetry of a curve. Positive values mean the bulk
  400 |         of the values are on the left side of the average and vice versa.
  401 | 
  402 |         http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skewness
  403 | 
  404 |         See the module docstring for more about statistical moments.
  405 | 
  406 |         >>> skewness(range(97))  # symmetrical around 48.0
  407 |         0.0
  408 |         >>> left_skewed = skewness(list(range(97)) + list(range(10)))
  409 |         >>> right_skewed = skewness(list(range(97)) + list(range(87, 97)))
  410 |         >>> round(left_skewed, 3), round(right_skewed, 3)
  411 |         (0.114, -0.114)

  413 |         data, s_dev = self.data, self.std_dev
  414 |         if len(data) > 1 and s_dev > 0:
  415 |             return (sum(self._get_pow_diffs(3)) /
  416 |                     float((len(data) - 1) * (s_dev ** 3)))
  417 |         else:
  418 |             return self.default
  419 |     skewness = _StatsProperty('skewness', _calc_skewness)

  421 |     def _calc_kurtosis(self):

  423 |         Indicates how much data is in the tails of the distribution. The
  424 |         result is always positive, with the normal "bell-curve"
  425 |         distribution having a kurtosis of 3.
  426 | 
  427 |         http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kurtosis
  428 | 
  429 |         See the module docstring for more about statistical moments.
  430 | 
  431 |         >>> kurtosis(range(9))
  432 |         1.99125

  434 |         With a kurtosis of 1.99125, [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8] is more
  435 |         centrally distributed than the normal curve.
  436 |         """
  437 |         data, s_dev = self.data, self.std_dev
  438 |         if len(data) > 1 and s_dev > 0:
  439 |             return (sum(self._get_pow_diffs(4)) /
  440 |                     float((len(data) - 1) * (s_dev ** 4)))
  441 |         else:
  442 |             return 0.0
  443 |     kurtosis = _StatsProperty('kurtosis', _calc_kurtosis)

  445 |     def _calc_pearson_type(self):
  446 |         precision = self._pearson_precision
  447 |         skewness = self.skewness
  448 |         kurtosis = self.kurtosis
  449 |         beta1 = skewness ** 2.0
  450 |         beta2 = kurtosis * 1.0
  451 | 
  452 |         # TODO: range checks?
  453 | 
  454 |         c0 = (4 * beta2) - (3 * beta1)
  455 |         c1 = skewness * (beta2 + 3)
  456 |         c2 = (2 * beta2) - (3 * beta1) - 6
  457 | 
  458 |         if round(c1, precision) == 0:
  459 |             if round(beta2, precision) == 3:
  460 |                 return 0  # Normal
  461 |             else:
  462 |                 if beta2 < 3:
  463 |                     return 2  # Symmetric Beta
  464 |                 elif beta2 > 3:
  465 |                     return 7
  466 |         elif round(c2, precision) == 0:
  467 |             return 3  # Gamma
  468 |         else:
  469 |             if c0 == 0:
  470 |                 # At exact zero, c2's sign selects the limiting Type I/VI.
  471 |                 return 1 if c2 < 0 else 6
  472 |             k = c1 ** 2 / (4 * c0 * c2)
  473 |             if k < 0:
  474 |                 return 1  # Beta
  475 |             # The existing precision also widens the Type V boundary.
  476 |             elif round(k, precision) == 1:
  477 |                 return 5  # Type V
  478 |             elif k < 1:
  479 |                 return 4  # Type IV
  480 |             else:
  481 |                 return 6  # Type VI
  482 |         raise RuntimeError('missed a spot')

  485 |     @staticmethod
  486 |     def _get_quantile(sorted_data, q):
  487 |         data, n = sorted_data, len(sorted_data)
  488 |         idx = q / 1.0 * (n - 1)
  489 |         idx_f, idx_c = int(floor(idx)), int(ceil(idx))
  490 |         if idx_f == idx_c:
  491 |             return data[idx_f]
  492 |         return (data[idx_f] * (idx_c - idx)) + (data[idx_c] * (idx - idx_f))
  493 | 
  494 |     def get_quantile(self, q):
  495 |         """Get a quantile from the dataset. Quantiles are floating point
  496 |         values between ``0.0`` and ``1.0``, with ``0.0`` representing
  497 |         the minimum value in the dataset and ``1.0`` representing the
  498 |         maximum. ``0.5`` represents the median:
  499 | 
  500 |         >>> Stats(range(100)).get_quantile(0.5)
  501 |         49.5
  502 |         """
  503 |         q = float(q)
  504 |         if not 0.0 <= q <= 1.0:
  505 |             raise ValueError('expected q between 0.0 and 1.0, not %r' % q)
  506 |         elif not self.data:
  507 |             return self.default
  508 |         return self._get_quantile(self._get_sorted_data(), q)
  509 | 
  510 |     def get_zscore(self, value):
  511 |         """Get the z-score for *value* in the group. If the standard deviation
  512 |         is 0, 0 inf or -inf will be returned to indicate whether the value is
  513 |         equal to, greater than or below the group's mean.
  514 |         """
  515 |         mean = self.mean
  516 |         if self.std_dev == 0:
  517 |             if value == mean:
  518 |                 return 0
  519 |             if value > mean:
  520 |                 return float('inf')
  521 |             if value < mean:
  522 |                 return float('-inf')
  523 |         return (float(value) - mean) / self.std_dev
  524 | 
  525 |     def trim_relative(self, amount=0.15):
  526 |         """A utility function used to cut a proportion of values off each end
  527 |         of a list of values. This has the effect of limiting the
  528 |         effect of outliers.
  529 | 
  530 |         Args:
  531 |             amount (float): A value between 0.0 and 0.5 to trim off of
  532 |                 each side of the data.
  533 | 
  534 |         .. note:
  535 | 
  536 |             This operation modifies the data in-place. It does not
  537 |             make or return a copy.
  538 | 
  539 |         """
  540 |         trim = float(amount)
  541 |         if not 0.0 <= trim < 0.5:
  542 |             raise ValueError('expected amount between 0.0 and 0.5, not %r'
  543 |                              % trim)
  544 |         size = len(self.data)
  545 |         size_diff = int(size * trim)
  546 |         if size_diff == 0.0:
  547 |             return
  548 |         self.data = self._get_sorted_data()[size_diff:-size_diff]
  549 |         self.clear_cache()
  550 | 
  551 |     def _get_pow_diffs(self, power):
  552 |         """
  553 |         A utility function used for calculating statistical moments.
  554 |         """
  555 |         m = self.mean
  556 |         return [(v - m) ** power for v in self.data]

  558 |     def _get_bin_bounds(self, count=None, with_max=False):
  559 |         if not self.data:
  560 |             return [0.0]  # TODO: raise?
  561 | 
  562 |         data = self.data
  563 |         len_data, min_data, max_data = len(data), min(data), max(data)
  564 | 
  565 |         if len_data < 4:
  566 |             if not count:
  567 |                 count = len_data
  568 |             dx = (max_data - min_data) / float(count)
  569 |             bins = [min_data + (dx * i) for i in range(count)]
  570 |         elif count is None:
  571 |             # freedman algorithm for fixed-width bin selection
  572 |             q25, q75 = self.get_quantile(0.25), self.get_quantile(0.75)
  573 |             dx = 2 * (q75 - q25) / (len_data ** (1 / 3.0))
  574 |             if dx == 0:
  575 |                 return [float(min_data), float(max_data)] if with_max else [float(min_data)]
  576 |             bin_count = max(1, int(ceil((max_data - min_data) / dx)))
  577 |             bins = [min_data + (dx * i) for i in range(bin_count + 1)]
  578 |             bins = [b for b in bins if b < max_data]
  579 |         else:
  580 |             dx = (max_data - min_data) / float(count)
  581 |             bins = [min_data + (dx * i) for i in range(count)]
  582 | 
  583 |         if with_max:
  584 |             bins.append(float(max_data))
  585 | 
  586 |         return bins

  588 |     def get_histogram_counts(self, bins=None, **kw):
  589 |         """Produces a list of ``(bin, count)`` pairs comprising a histogram of
  590 |         the Stats object's data, using fixed-width bins. See
  591 |         :meth:`Stats.format_histogram` for more details.
  592 | 
  593 |         Args:
  594 |             bins (int): maximum number of bins, or list of
  595 |                 floating-point bin boundaries. Defaults to the output of
  596 |                 Freedman's algorithm.
  597 |             bin_digits (int): Number of digits used to round down the
  598 |                 bin boundaries. Defaults to 1.
  599 | 
  600 |         The output of this method can be stored and/or modified, and
  601 |         then passed to :func:`statsutils.format_histogram_counts` to
  602 |         achieve the same text formatting as the
  603 |         :meth:`~Stats.format_histogram` method. This can be useful for
  604 |         snapshotting over time.
  605 |         """
  606 |         bin_digits = int(kw.pop('bin_digits', 1))
  607 |         if kw:
  608 |             raise TypeError('unexpected keyword arguments: %r' % kw.keys())
  609 | 
  610 |         if not bins:
  611 |             bins = self._get_bin_bounds()
  612 |         else:
  613 |             try:
  614 |                 bin_count = int(bins)
  615 |             except TypeError:
  616 |                 try:
  617 |                     bins = [float(x) for x in bins]
  618 |                 except Exception:
  619 |                     raise ValueError('bins expected integer bin count or list'
  620 |                                      ' of float bin boundaries, not %r' % bins)
  621 |                 if self.min < bins[0]:
  622 |                     bins = [self.min] + bins
  623 |             else:
  624 |                 bins = self._get_bin_bounds(bin_count)
  625 | 
  626 |         # floor and ceil really should have taken ndigits, like round()
  627 |         round_factor = 10.0 ** bin_digits
  628 |         bins = [floor(b * round_factor) / round_factor for b in bins]
  629 |         bins = sorted(set(bins))
  630 | 
  631 |         idxs = [bisect.bisect(bins, d) - 1 for d in self.data]
  632 |         count_map = Counter(idxs)
  633 | 
  634 |         bin_counts = [(b, count_map.get(i, 0)) for i, b in enumerate(bins)]
  635 | 
  636 |         return bin_counts
  637 | 
  638 |     def format_histogram(self, bins=None, **kw):
  639 |         """Produces a textual histogram of the data, using fixed-width bins,
  640 |         allowing for simple visualization, even in console environments.
  641 | 
  642 |         >>> data = list(range(20)) + list(range(5, 15)) + [10]
  643 |         >>> print(Stats(data).format_histogram(width=30))
  644 |          0.0:  5 #########
  645 |          4.4:  8 ###############
  646 |          8.9: 11 ####################
  647 |         13.3:  5 #########
  648 |         17.8:  2 ####
  649 | 
  650 |         In this histogram, five values are between 0.0 and 4.4, eight
  651 |         are between 4.4 and 8.9, and two values lie between 17.8 and
  652 |         the max.
  653 | 
  654 |         You can specify the number of bins, or provide a list of
  655 |         bin boundaries themselves. If no bins are provided, as in the
  656 |         example above, `Freedman's algorithm`_ for bin selection is
  657 |         used.
  658 | 
  659 |         Args:
  660 |             bins (int): Maximum number of bins for the
  661 |                 histogram. Also accepts a list of floating-point
  662 |                 bin boundaries. If the minimum boundary is still
  663 |                 greater than the minimum value in the data, that
  664 |                 boundary will be implicitly added. Defaults to the bin
  665 |                 boundaries returned by `Freedman's algorithm`_.
  666 |             bin_digits (int): Number of digits to round each bin
  667 |                 to. Note that bins are always rounded down to avoid
  668 |                 clipping any data. Defaults to 1.
  669 |             width (int): integer number of columns in the longest line
  670 |                in the histogram. Defaults to console width on Python
  671 |                3.3+, or 80 if that is not available.
  672 |             format_bin (callable): Called on each bin to create a
  673 |                label for the final output. Use this function to add
  674 |                units, such as "ms" for milliseconds.
  675 | 
  676 |         Should you want something more programmatically reusable, see
  677 |         the :meth:`~Stats.get_histogram_counts` method, the output of
  678 |         is used by format_histogram. The :meth:`~Stats.describe`
  679 |         method is another useful summarization method, albeit less
  680 |         visual.
  681 | 
  682 |         .. _Freedman's algorithm: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedman%E2%80%93Diaconis_rule
  683 |         """
  684 |         width = kw.pop('width', None)
  685 |         format_bin = kw.pop('format_bin', None)
  686 |         bin_counts = self.get_histogram_counts(bins=bins, **kw)
  687 |         return format_histogram_counts(bin_counts,
  688 |                                        width=width,

import math

import pytest

from boltons.statsutils import (
    Stats,
    describe,
    format_histogram_counts,
    mean,
    median,
    mode,

    skewness,
    kurtosis,
    trimean,
    iqr,
    pearson_type,
)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Stats basics: construction, len, iter
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def test_stats_len_and_iter():
    s = Stats([1, 2, 3, 4])
    assert len(s) == 4
    assert list(s) == [1, 2, 3, 4]


def test_stats_copies_data_by_default():
    data = [3, 1, 2]
    s = Stats(data)
    assert s.data == [3, 1, 2]
    assert s.data is not data
    # mutating original doesn't affect stats
    data.append(100)
    assert s.data == [3, 1, 2]


def test_stats_use_copy_false_shares_data():
    data = [3, 1, 2]
    s = Stats(data, use_copy=False)
    assert s.data is data


def test_stats_default_value():
    s = Stats([], default=float('nan'))
    assert math.isnan(s.default)
    assert math.isnan(s.mean)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Basic Stats properties
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def test_count():
    assert Stats(range(20)).count == 20


def test_mean_property():
    assert Stats(range(42)).mean == 20.5


def test_min_max_property():
    s = Stats([2, 1, 3])
    assert s.min == 1
    assert s.max == 3


def test_min_max_sorted():
    s = Stats([1, 2, 3], is_sorted=True)
    assert s.min == 1
    assert s.max == 3


def test_median_property():
    assert Stats([2, 1, 3]).median == 2
    assert Stats(range(97)).median == 48


def test_mode_property():
    assert Stats([2, 1, 3, 1]).mode == 1
    assert Stats(['a', 'b', 'b', 'c', 'c', 'c']).mode == 'c'
    assert Stats([1, 1, 2, 2, 3]).mode == 1


def test_iqr_property():
    assert Stats([1, 2, 3, 4, 5]).iqr == 2
    assert Stats(range(1001)).iqr == 500


def test_trimean_property():
    assert Stats([2, 1, 3]).trimean == 2.0
    assert Stats(range(97)).trimean == 48.0


def test_variance_property():
    assert Stats(range(97)).variance == 784.0


def test_std_dev_property():
    assert Stats(range(97)).std_dev == 28.0


def test_median_abs_dev_property():
    assert Stats(range(97)).median_abs_dev == 24.0
    # mad alias
    assert Stats(range(97)).mad == 24.0


def test_rel_std_dev_property():
    s = Stats(range(97))
    assert abs(s.rel_std_dev - (28.0 / 48.0)) < 1e-12


def test_rel_std_dev_zero_mean_returns_default():
    s = Stats([-1, 1], default=123.0)
    assert s.mean == 0.0
    assert s.rel_std_dev == 123.0


def test_skewness_property():
    assert Stats(range(97)).skewness == 0.0


def test_skewness_default_when_single_value():
    s = Stats([5], default=-1.0)
    assert s.skewness == -1.0


def test_kurtosis_property():
    assert Stats(range(9)).kurtosis == 1.99125


def test_kurtosis_single_value_zero():
    assert Stats([5]).kurtosis == 0.0


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Module-level convenience functions
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def test_module_level_mean():
    assert mean(range(42)) == 20.5


def test_module_level_median():
    assert median([2, 1, 3]) == 2
    assert median(range(97)) == 48


def test_module_level_mode():
    assert mode([2, 1, 3, 1]) == 1


def test_module_level_variance_std_dev():
    assert variance(range(97)) == 784.0
    assert std_dev(range(97)) == 28.0


def test_module_level_median_abs_dev():
    assert median_abs_dev(range(97)) == 24.0


def test_module_level_rel_std_dev():
    assert abs(rel_std_dev(range(97)) - (28.0 / 48.0)) < 1e-12


def test_module_level_skewness_kurtosis():
    assert skewness(range(97)) == 0.0
    assert kurtosis(range(9)) == 1.99125


def test_module_level_trimean_iqr():
    assert trimean(range(97)) == 48.0
    assert iqr(range(1001)) == 500


def test_module_level_pearson_type():
    # just exercise the function
    assert pearson_type(range(97)) in {0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7}


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Caching / clear_cache
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def test_cache_set_on_access():
    s = Stats(range(10))
    assert not hasattr(s, '_mean')
    _ = s.mean
    assert hasattr(s, '_mean')
    assert s._mean == s.mean


def test_clear_cache():
    s = Stats(range(10))
    _ = s.mean
    _ = s.variance
    assert hasattr(s, '_mean')
    assert hasattr(s, '_variance')
    s.clear_cache()
    assert not hasattr(s, '_mean')
    assert not hasattr(s, '_variance')


def test_clear_cache_recomputes():
    s = Stats([1, 2, 3])
    assert s.mean == 2.0
    s.data.append(10)
    s.clear_cache()
    assert s.mean == 4.0

    assert Stats(range(100)).get_quantile(0.5) == 49.5


def test_get_quantile_min_max():

    assert s.get_quantile(0.0) == 0
    assert s.get_quantile(1.0) == 9


def test_get_quantile_empty_returns_default():

    assert s.get_quantile(0.5) == 42.0


def test_get_quantile_out_of_range():
    s = Stats(range(10))
    with pytest.raises(ValueError):

    with pytest.raises(ValueError):
        s.get_quantile(-0.1)


def test_get_quantile_accepts_string():

    s = Stats(range(10))
    assert s.get_quantile('0.5') == 4.5

def test_get_zscore_zero_stddev_equal():
    s = Stats([5, 5, 5])
    assert s.get_zscore(5) == 0


def test_get_zscore_zero_stddev_greater():
    s = Stats([5, 5, 5])
    assert s.get_zscore(10) == float('inf')


def test_get_zscore_zero_stddev_less():
    s = Stats([5, 5, 5])
    assert s.get_zscore(1) == float('-inf')


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def test_trim_relative_modifies_in_place():
    s = Stats(range(10))
    s.trim_relative(0.1)
    assert s.data == [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8]


def test_trim_relative_noop_when_small():
    s = Stats(range(3))
    s.trim_relative(0.1)
    assert s.data == [0, 1, 2]


def test_trim_relative_invalid():
    s = Stats(range(10))
    with pytest.raises(ValueError):
        s.trim_relative(0.5)
    with pytest.raises(ValueError):
        s.trim_relative(-0.1)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def test_get_histogram_counts_empty():
    s = Stats([])
    assert s.get_histogram_counts() == [(0.0, 0)]


def test_get_histogram_counts_with_bin_count():
    s = Stats(range(10))
    result = s.get_histogram_counts(bins=2)
    assert len(result) == 2
    # all counts sum to number of data points
    assert sum(c for _, c in result) == 10


def test_get_histogram_counts_with_bin_list():
    s = Stats(range(10))
    result = s.get_histogram_counts(bins=[0.0, 5.0, 9.0])
    assert sum(c for _, c in result) == 10


def test_get_histogram_counts_adds_min():
    s = Stats([2, 3, 4])
    # min is 2, passing bins starting at 3 should prepend min
    result = s.get_histogram_counts(bins=[3.0, 4.0])
    assert result[0][0] == 2.0


def test_get_histogram_counts_unexpected_kw():
    s = Stats(range(10))
    with pytest.raises(TypeError):
        s.get_histogram_counts(foo=1)


def test_format_histogram():
    data = list(range(20)) + list(range(5, 15)) + [10]
    out = Stats(data).format_histogram(width=30)
    assert isinstance(out, str)
    # five lines expected from the docstring example
    lines = out.splitlines()
    assert len(lines) == 5


def test_format_histogram_counts_basic():
    bin_counts = [(0.0, 5), (5.0, 10), (10.0, 3)]
    out = format_histogram_counts(bin_counts, width=40)
    lines = out.splitlines()
    assert len(lines) == 3
    # Each line should contain colon and a count
    assert '0.0:' in lines[0]
    assert '5.0:' in lines[1]
    assert '10.0:' in lines[2]


def test_format_histogram_counts_zero_count_uses_pipe():
    bin_counts = [(0.0, 0), (1.0, 5)]
    out = format_histogram_counts(bin_counts, width=40)
    lines = out.splitlines()
    # zero count line should contain '|'

   31 | """``statsutils`` provides tools aimed primarily at descriptive
   32 | statistics for data analysis, such as :func:`mean` (average),
   33 | :func:`median`, :func:`mode`, :func:`variance`, and many others,
   34 | 
   35 | The :class:`Stats` type provides all the main functionality of the
   36 | ``statsutils`` module. A :class:`Stats` object wraps a given dataset,
   37 | providing all statistical measures as property attributes. These
   38 | attributes cache their results, which allows efficient computation of
   39 | multiple measures, as many measures rely on other measures. For
   40 | example, relative standard deviation (:attr:`Stats.rel_std_dev`)
   41 | relies on both the mean and standard deviation. The Stats object
   42 | caches those results so no rework is done.
   43 | 
   44 | The :class:`Stats` type's attributes have module-level counterparts for
   45 | convenience when the computation reuse advantages do not apply.
   46 | 
   47 | >>> stats = Stats(range(42))
   48 | >>> stats.mean
   49 | 20.5
   50 | >>> mean(range(42))
   51 | 20.5
   52 | 
   53 | Statistics is a large field, and ``statsutils`` is focused on a few
   54 | basic techniques that are useful in software. The following is a brief
   55 | introduction to those techniques. For a more in-depth introduction,
   56 | `Statistics for Software
   57 | <https://www.paypal-engineering.com/2016/04/11/statistics-for-software/>`_,
   58 | an article I wrote on the topic. It introduces key terminology vital
   59 | to effective usage of statistics.
   60 | 
   61 | Statistical moments
   62 | -------------------
   63 | 
   64 | Python programmers are probably familiar with the concept of the
   65 | *mean* or *average*, which gives a rough quantitiative middle value by
   66 | which a sample can be can be generalized. However, the mean is just
   67 | the first of four `moment`_-based measures by which a sample or
   68 | distribution can be measured.
   69 | 
   70 | The four `Standardized moments`_ are:
   71 | 
   72 |   1. `Mean`_ - :func:`mean` - theoretical middle value
   73 |   2. `Variance`_ - :func:`variance` - width of value dispersion
   74 |   3. `Skewness`_ - :func:`skewness` - symmetry of distribution
   75 |   4. `Kurtosis`_ - :func:`kurtosis` - "peakiness" or "long-tailed"-ness
   76 | 
   77 | For more information check out `the Moment article on Wikipedia`_.
   78 | 
   79 | .. _moment: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moment_(mathematics)
   80 | .. _Standardized moments: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standardized_moment
   81 | .. _Mean: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mean
   82 | .. _Variance: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Variance
   83 | .. _Skewness: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skewness
   84 | .. _Kurtosis: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kurtosis
   85 | .. _the Moment article on Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moment_(mathematics)
   86 | 
   87 | Keep in mind that while these moments can give a bit more insight into
   88 | the shape and distribution of data, they do not guarantee a complete
   89 | picture. Wildly different datasets can have the same values for all
   90 | four moments, so generalize wisely.
   91 | 
   92 | Robust statistics
   93 | -----------------
   94 | 
   95 | Moment-based statistics are notorious for being easily skewed by
   96 | outliers. The whole field of robust statistics aims to mitigate this
   97 | dilemma. ``statsutils`` also includes several robust statistical methods:
   98 | 
   99 |   * `Median`_ - The middle value of a sorted dataset
  100 |   * `Trimean`_ - Another robust measure of the data's central tendency
  101 |   * `Median Absolute Deviation`_ (MAD) - A robust measure of
  102 |     variability, a natural counterpart to :func:`variance`.
  103 |   * `Trimming`_ - Reducing a dataset to only the middle majority of
  104 |     data is a simple way of making other estimators more robust.
  105 | 
  106 | .. _Median: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Median
  107 | .. _Trimean: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trimean
  108 | .. _Median Absolute Deviation: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Median_absolute_deviation
  109 | .. _Trimming: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trimmed_estimator
  110 | 
  111 | 
  112 | Online and Offline Statistics
  113 | -----------------------------
  114 | 
  115 | Unrelated to computer networking, `online`_ statistics involve
  116 | calculating statistics in a `streaming`_ fashion, without all the data
  117 | being available. The :class:`Stats` type is meant for the more
  118 | traditional offline statistics when all the data is available. For
  119 | pure-Python online statistics accumulators, look at the `Lithoxyl`_
  120 | system instrumentation package.
  121 | 
  122 | .. _Online: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Online_algorithm
  123 | .. _streaming: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Streaming_algorithm
  124 | .. _Lithoxyl: https://github.com/mahmoud/lithoxyl
  125 |

  135 |     def __init__(self, name, func):

  137 |         self.func = func
  138 |         self.internal_name = '_' + name
  139 | 
  140 |         doc = func.__doc__ or ''
  141 |         pre_doctest_doc, _, _ = doc.partition('>>>')
  142 |         self.__doc__ = pre_doctest_doc

  144 |     def __get__(self, obj, objtype=None):

  146 |             return self
  147 |         if not obj.data:
  148 |             return obj.default
  149 |         try:
  150 |             return getattr(obj, self.internal_name)
  151 |         except AttributeError:
  152 |             setattr(obj, self.internal_name, self.func(obj))
